title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
directAnswer: A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot still has the property that at any mid, at least one of the two halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is fully sorted. In one binary search, figure out which half is sorted, test whether the target falls inside that sorted half's value range, and discard the half that can't contain it. O(log n) time, O(1) space — no need to find the pivot first.

remember.formula:
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target: return mid
    if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:        # left half sorted
        if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]: hi = mid - 1
        else: lo = mid + 1
    else:                            # right half sorted
        if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
return -1
rules: At every mid, compare `nums[lo]` to `nums[mid]` — if `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` the **left** half is sorted, otherwise the **right** half is.
Use `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` so the single-element case (`lo == mid`) is treated as a sorted left half.
Only commit to a half after checking the target lies *within that sorted half's value bounds*; otherwise search the other half.
Use the same overflow-safe `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` and inclusive `while (lo <= hi)` as plain binary search.
You do **not** need to find the pivot first — one pass handles rotation directly.
whenToUse: A sorted array was rotated by an unknown amount and you need O(log n) lookup
Any 'piecewise sorted / one discontinuity' array where half is always clean
Follow-ups that combine rotation with search (find min, find pivot, search with duplicates)
antiSignals: Array isn't rotated → plain binary search, no half-check needed
Duplicates are allowed (LeetCode 81) → `nums[lo] == nums[mid]` is ambiguous; shrink lo by one, worst case O(n)
You need the rotation count itself → that's Find Minimum, a simpler mid-vs-hi compare
remember.takeaway: The whole trick is that rotation creates exactly one 'break point', so one of the two halves around any mid is always a clean sorted range you can range-test against. Recognising 'at least one half is sorted' generalises to every rotated-array variant.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can adapt the binary-search invariant to a non-monotonic array by reasoning about which half stays sorted, instead of giving up and scanning linearly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing only nums[mid] to target (plain binary search) and ignoring rotation, or getting the boundary `<=` wrong so a target equal to nums[lo] or nums[hi] is dropped.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain *why* one half is always sorted (a single rotation = one discontinuity), then write the four-way branch carefully and dry-run a case where the target is in the unsorted half.

problemStatement:
There is an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order (with **distinct** values). Prior to being passed to your function, `nums` is possibly **rotated** at an unknown pivot index `k` (`0 <= k < nums.length`) so that the resulting array is `[nums[k], nums[k+1], ..., nums[n-1], nums[0], nums[1], ..., nums[k-1]]`.

Given the array `nums` after the possible rotation and an integer `target`, return the **index** of `target` if it is in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique
nums is an ascending array possibly rotated
understanding: Take a sorted array and cut it once, swapping the two pieces — that's a rotation. The array now has one 'drop' (where the larger end meets the smaller start). Despite the drop, any midpoint splits the array such that one side is a contiguous sorted run. We use that to keep halving.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values guaranteed distinct?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes here. Duplicates (LeetCode 81) break the `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` test when they're equal and force a worst-case O(n) fallback.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the array be un-rotated (rotated by 0 or n)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — k can be 0, which means a normal sorted array. The same code handles it: the left half is always detected as sorted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to find the pivot index first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Finding the pivot then searching is a valid two-pass O(log n) approach, but the one-pass 'which half is sorted' method is cleaner and what interviewers look for.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do I return when the target is absent?

Walk the array and return the first index whose value equals the target, else `-1`.

**Why mention it.** It's a correctness anchor and a complexity to beat. **Why it's wrong here.** The prompt requires `O(log n)`; a scan ignores the structure (sorted, single rotation) that lets us halve the search.
approaches.insight: Rotation feels like it destroys sortedness, but it only introduces *one* discontinuity. A linear scan throws away that structure; binary search exploits it.

Assuming you must locate the pivot to do better — you don't.

approaches.name: One-Pass Binary Search — Which Half Is Sorted (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer. Lead with 'one half around mid is always sorted' to show the key insight before coding.
hints: Picture cutting a sorted array once and swapping the pieces. Around any middle index, is it possible for BOTH halves to be broken at the same time?
Exactly one half [lo..mid] or [mid..hi] is a clean sorted run. Detect it by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid].
If the sorted half's value range brackets the target, recurse into it; otherwise recurse into the other half. Keep the inclusive [lo, hi] template.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration discards half the window with O(1) work, so O(log n) iterations and O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Run a standard binary search, but augment the mid step to cope with rotation.

**The structural fact.** A single rotation of a sorted array creates exactly *one* point where a larger value is immediately followed by a smaller one. For any `mid`, the break point lies in at most one of the two halves `[lo, mid]` and `[mid, hi]` — so the *other* half is a contiguous sorted run. That guarantees that at every step at least one half is sorted, and we can reason about it precisely.

**Detecting the sorted half.** Compare `nums[lo]` with `nums[mid]`. If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, the left half `[lo, mid]` is sorted (no break between them). Otherwise the break is on the left, which means the right half `[mid, hi]` is the sorted one. The `<=` matters: when `lo == mid` (window of size 1 or 2) the left half is trivially 'sorted', and `<=` keeps that case in the left branch.

**Range-testing the target.** Once we know which half is sorted, we know its exact value bounds, so we can ask in O(1) whether the target lies inside it. If the **left** half is sorted and `nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]`, the target — if present — must be in the left half, so set `hi = mid - 1`; otherwise it must be in the right half, so `lo = mid + 1`. Symmetrically, if the **right** half is sorted and `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]`, search right (`lo = mid + 1`), else search left (`hi = mid - 1`).

**Why the boundary comparisons use the asymmetric `<` / `<=`.** We've already returned if `nums[mid] == target`, so mid itself is excluded. On the sorted *left* half the inclusive end is `nums[lo]` (could equal target) and the exclusive end is `nums[mid]` — hence `nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]`. On the sorted *right* half it mirrors: `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]`. Getting these endpoints right is what separates a correct solution from one that drops targets sitting exactly at `lo` or `hi`.

**Termination and absence.** The window strictly shrinks every iteration (we always move past mid), so the loop ends; if it exits, the target isn't there and we return `-1`.
approaches.insight: You never need to know *where* the pivot is — only which side of `mid` is currently clean. That reframing (local sortedness, not global structure) is the reusable idea: it reappears in Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array and in the duplicates variant, where the only change is how you break the `nums[lo] == nums[mid]` tie.

No break between lo and mid → the LEFT half is the sorted run. `<=` covers lo == mid.

Discard mid and everything right of it.
Target not in the sorted left half → it can only be on the right.
nums[lo] > nums[mid] → the break is on the left, so the RIGHT half is sorted.
Target within the sorted right half's range → search right.

Target inside the sorted right range → go right.

pitfalls: Using `<` instead of `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` — mishandles the lo == mid window.
Wrong endpoint inclusivity in the range tests — drops targets equal to nums[lo] or nums[hi].
Trying to handle duplicates with this exact code — equal nums[lo]/nums[mid] is ambiguous and needs a separate shrink step.
Range-testing against the *unsorted* half, whose bounds don't bracket its contents.

commonMistakes: Comparing only nums[mid] to target and forgetting the array is rotated.
Getting the inclusive/exclusive endpoints wrong in the range checks, dropping targets at the boundaries.
Assuming this code handles duplicates — it requires distinct values.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Range-testing against the wrong (unsorted) half
commonMistakesDetailed.why: You can only reason about value bounds on the SORTED half. Checking the target against the unsorted half's endpoints gives meaningless comparisons and wrong branches.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict vs non-strict boundary
commonMistakesDetailed.why: mid is already excluded (we returned on equality), but lo and hi are not. Using `<` on the inclusive end drops a target equal to nums[lo] or nums[hi].
